newsitem.title: USA: Huang to pursue immunity in U.S. campaign probe.
newsitem.headline: Huang to pursue immunity in U.S. campaign probe.

text.p: John Huang, a key figure in alleged Democrat fundraising abuses, will pursue his offer to testify before a Senate panel in return for limited immunity despite a cool initial response, his lawyer said on Thursday.

"I'm becoming very discouraged but i'm not prepared to throw in the towel yet," Huang's lawer Ty Cobb told MSNBC. He is to meet lawyers from both parties Friday to determine whether Republican majority leaders, who have cited Huang as a key potential witness, have "any real interest in exploring this possibility."

Huang raised $3.4 million in nine months working for the Democratic National Committee before last year's presidential election, but almost half of that was returned by the DNC after reports that it was improperly raised from foreigners.

Huang's offer to testify before the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee was dramatically disclosed when the televised hearings opened Tuesday. He dropped his refusal to speak on the grounds that he might incriminate himself, but only on condition he be given immunity from prosecution on possible violations of campaign finance laws or other charges except espionage and passing secrets to foreign countries.

Republicans on the committee expressed scepticism and the chairman, Tennessee Republican Sen. Fred Thompson, said he had been told by the Justice Department that it opposed any immunity for Huang. Justice officials said privately they feared this would interfere with a separate department task force investigation.
Sen. John Glenn of Ohio, the committee's senior Democrat, said he hoped the committee can "figure out a way to give (Huang) protection in fairly small areas" so he can give his side of the story.
Committee members said Cobb should submit a description of what Huang is prepared to tell the committee in return for limited immunity.

Laurence Walsh, the special prosecutor who investigated the Iran-Contra scandal under President Ronald Reagan in the 1980s and who says his case was severely damaged by immunity offers then, urged caution. "You can't rush the process, you're dealing with hostile witnesses. It will be harmful, both to the committee and to the Justice Department, if immunity is given prematurely," he told MSNBC.

"The premature granting of immunity" by a Senate committee to two key figures, Oliver North and Adm. John Poindexter, "ultimately destroyed our prosecution," Walsh said. "We successfully convicted them of felonies but the Court of Appeals reversed because of the immunity given by Congress."

In the Iran-Contra affair, the White House arranged for the sale of weapons to Iran and the diversion of profits to the Nicaraguan Contra rebels despite a congressional ban on such military assistance.
